utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon and Salvatore Cannata for the Prosecution. Ms. Javier has been delayed by the inclement weather, and she will join us during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the participants in the proceedings. General Perisic is represented today by Boris Zorko and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good morning, Mr. Novakovic. Just to remind you that you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Now that -- actually, now when you walked into the courtroom I think that you tried to tell me something and I think that I understood what you were trying to say; however, we are not allowed to communicate. So could you please address the Court. Could you please say what it was. I think that it was due to the air-conditioning that you've started coughing or something, the air-conditioning in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I have a bit of a throat problem, but it's meaningless really.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nothing is meaningless, Mr. Novakovic. If you do not feel well, as I indicated at the beginning of your testimony yesterday, please do indicate, and let's see what we can do to help. If -- I don't know whether we can switch off the air con, but we might perhaps give you a break to go and get fresh air outside, if it happens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I think that we can consider the situation to be normal. If I cough a bit every now and then, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This just reminded me of something that I heard from witnesses after their testimony. I just remember that. They told me that where they sat - I can't remember whether it was in this courtroom though - but they had the air-conditioning blowing right into them. Maybe it was in another courtroom. Never mind. They said that they felt this flow of air coming right at them. I think it was Witness Nikolic, but that is no reason for any objections or any kind of dialogue with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, let us continue where we broke off yesterday. I would just like to go back to a topic that I omitted yesterday because I did not have the adequate translation. So we're going to go back into the past again, the period of the autumn of 1991, or rather, more specifically, December 1991, when you were part of the 1st Operations Group that was sent by the SSNO to the territory of Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P1196 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we can see, this document is the Law on Defence and it was promulgated by the government. I think that the Trial Chamber does not have the first page of the document before them, but what is written on the first page is that the Government of the SAO Krajina passed a Law on Defence on the 2nd of December, 1991. The Prosecution tendered a few articles of this law. This is a voluminous document. It has quite a few articles, about 150 or 120. I would be interested in Article 31. I think that that is one of the articles that the Prosecution tendered into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] B/C/S page is page 6, page 6 of the document. In English it starts at the end of page 2 and continues on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I'm interested in the first paragraph. Please read it to yourself, the first paragraph of Article 31?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we discussed this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, could the next page in English be brought up so that the Trial Chamber can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence that, on the basis of this law became - if I can put it that way - part of the system of the then-Serb autonomous region of the SAO Krajina on the 2nd of December, 1991. According to this particular regulation and according to the contacts you had then with the members of the TO staffs at the time, what do they consider themselves to be? Were they part of the single system of defence and armed forces of the SFRY or did they consider themselves to be something separate?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual practice was - and that was the understanding that people had in the Territorial Defence - that they were, as was the case until then, on the basis of regulations, part of the single armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to -- now I would like to look at Article 34. In the B/C/S it's the same page, and I'm going to call up the English translation because that article was not admitted into evidence when the Prosecution tendered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like to call up Article 34 as ET 1D12-0969.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a draft translation, may I say. General, I'm interested in the first paragraph -- actually, the entire article. I would like to hear your comment. In actual fact, you testified about this yesterday. This has to do with control and command in this Territorial Defence. You said that there were staffs and units in the Territorial Defence. According to this article here, it says that command and control in the Territorial Defence has to do with the fact that these staffs command the TO units. What was the situation in December 1991 in practice in relation to this provision of the law?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the autumn and winter of 1991, these staffs, where they had been established - and they had been established up to zone level and province level in the Serb autonomous region of Krajina - they did not directly command units. The units were directly commanded by the commands of the Yugoslav People's Army that were in a particular area. These staffs could not do that, they did not have the right conditions for doing that, and they didn't do so in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These TO units, these TO units that had been established according to the old system of the armed forces of the SFRY -- or actually, are we talking about some newly established TO units?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are units that were established according to the mobilisation plan that existed before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this is a draft translation, once we've received an official translation of this article, perhaps we could just attach that to the existing P exhibit. Otherwise, in B/C/S Article 34 that I'm interested in is already part of this exhibit in B/C/S. So that is what I'm primarily interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You're not asking for anything. We'll hear you when you make your request in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, once I've received an official translation. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I don't need this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we're going to go back to what you testified yesterday. Yesterday we saw a document appointing you commander of the Serb Army of the Krajina general. It's October 1992. Can you tell us, General, what you did, what your first tasks were when you were appointed commander of the Serb Army of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first task was to tour the entire area of the Serb Republic of the Krajina to see the situation in the Territorial Defence and also the PJMs. Also, to see what kind of information existed about the enemy, to talk to the leaders of the Republic of the Serb Krajina about their expectations in relation to defence, and to carry out an analysis, together with my co-workers, of the possible ways in which the Serb Army of the Krajina could be organised. Several variants were involved. We had to deal with the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what were the moves that followed?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, all the solutions that were being offered to us as the possible ones had a serious constraint, and that constraint was the presence of UNPROFOR and our resolve not to go beyond the Vance Plan in any way. In practical terms, that meant that at that point in time, as regards the Serb Army of the Krajina, we were establishing it from an administrative and organisational point of view; we are setting it up in terms of personnel; we are making assessments of the possible ways in which the population in the territory of the Republic of the Serb Krajina could come under threat. And we did all of that in accordance with the rules covering military geographic assessments on the one hand; and on the other hand, we had to look at what we had available, what we had in our hands at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the establishment of the army being set up then; and if not then, when? And who did it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organisational order was written up then for establishing the Serb Army of the Krajina. That means that for the most part we proceeded from the situation that we actually found on the ground, what had already come to be in certain territories of the Republic of the Serb Krajina in the armed conflicts that had taken place until then. As for classical formations in terms of internal regulations - I mean as the book of establishment, that's where it always says what the name of the unit is, what the number is, what the military post code is, then the duties according to establishment, ranks according to establishment, and so on - we didn't do any of that then. The Main Staff didn't really have the resources to do that because it was undermanned itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how was the establishment organised? What was the organisational structure according to which the units of the Army of the Serbian Krajina were set up?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a corps-brigade organisational system, which was common at the time in most of the armies of the world except for the US army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And whose decision or whose idea was it to adopt such an organisational system for the Serbian Army of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was myself and my associates'.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D164 now, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, General, which structures became part of the Army of the Serbian Krajina in relation to the previous situation in the field? General, what comprised the Serbian Army of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of the Serbian Krajina comprised the staffs of the TO, units -- the Posebne Jedinice Milicije, the PJMs, and the ranks were also replenished by all military conscripts, regardless of the fact whether they were in the TO or the PJM at the time, but were able-bodied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That organisation that you devised at the time, what was the estimate of the strength of the Army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We felt at the time that in the conditions where the people in the area of the Serbian Krajina were most in danger, the Army of the Serbian Krajina should number up to 80.000 men. But with maximum efforts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, we know what your wishes may have been. The question is: What was the strength? Not: What is the strength that you wished for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the army as such at that point in time did not exist. We were planning to form these units then, in the event of the imminent and open danger. And that is why on the basis of an incomplete insight into the demographic resources and the official census of the population in the municipalities, we felt that we could reach this number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But did there come a time when you did establish an army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when that time came, what was the strength of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are also including the PJMs and the TO staffs, that number ranged from 15- to 18.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Total army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that answer your question, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so because my question, Your Honour, Judge Moloto -- well, if you look at this line, I was going to go in order, and I was planning to put all of those questions to the witness. So line 18 on page 8, my -- my question was: What was the plan for the size of the army? And then I was going to put the questions that you have just put to the witness yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But this answer that you just gave, General, 15- to 18.000 men, at what point in time did the Army of the Serbian Krajina number that much?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the army was formed, and this number included the PJMs and all the municipal and area TO staffs as well as the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that point in time, in the next phase of the existence of the Army of the Serbian Krajina for as long as you were the commander of that army, in relation to the planned strength of 80.000, did you have a mobilisation, was there a response, were the units manned up to a larger number, the units of the Army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Croatian forces carried out an offensive, an attack, in the Maslenica inlet and the Ravni Kotari area and along the valley of the Cetina River from Sinj towards Glina, all that we had we mobilised, and that is when we approached that figure of 80.000, and that is when we took the weapons from the UNPROFOR depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will come to that question quite soon. But now that we're on this topic, I'm interested in the officer cadre of this Army of the Serbian Krajina, the commissioned and non-commissioned officer cadre. What was the plan, and how many men did you have at the begin? That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer and non-commissioned officer cadre in the Army of the Serbian Krajina mostly consisted of reserve-strength officers, both commissioned and non-commissioned officers from that area, and a slightly smaller number were officers and non-commissioned officers of the Yugoslav People's Army from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here in our court documents we do have some numbers. But what I'm interested in: In relation to the planned organisational structure of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, what was the percentage, in the beginning, of the planned number of officers and non-commissioned officers pursuant to this organisational structure?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that now we're going into an area where I really am not able to give you specific numbers, and this is why: We needed to have battalion commanders of the rank of major, those who had completed military academy. We just had 50 per cent of such officers as battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. Let us be precise. When you say "who completed the military academy," this is what we were talking about earlier, the professional cadre of the former JNA. I don't want to suggest anything to you, but that would be that, a person who completed military academy is somebody who is understood to be an active-duty professional military man. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be so because there was no other military academy in the area of the former Yugoslavia. If I may continue now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say now if we had the other 50 per cent of battalion commanders or not. I mean, all the battalions had commanders, but we had what we had. Some places, these were non-commissioned officers also who had proved themselves in battle and who had gained some kind of authority among the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "non-commissioned officer," do you mean active JNA non-commissioned officers or those who had been given that status within the Army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean both, Mr. Lukic, both. It wasn't important to us which one it was, particularly at that time, whether somebody had been in the JNA or not. The main thing was whether the person was fit for such duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we see a map now on the screen and it has some terms in English. But tell us, are you able to comment on this map? I'm interested in it in the sense that you were talking about in the corps-brigade organisation system of the Army of the Serbian Krajina. Can you tell us how the territorial organisation of those corps was, and was that the same situation that was in effect from the beginning until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were setting up the organisation of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, certain areas of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina - and you can see that on the map - we're talking about Northern Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can help and he can set up the marker for you so that you can point things out for us on the map.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Northern Dalmatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go in order. It says something here in the English language, what you wrote just now. What was that corps? What was its name? And was it there throughout the whole war?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I will skip a part of the answer, as you wish. So we have Northern Dalmatian where we had the 7th Corps in the Lika area, which was a topographic whole, there was the 15th Corps. In the Kordun area, the 21st Corps was formed. In the Banija area there was the 39th Corps that was formed. And then in Western Slavonia you had the 18th Corps. And then you had the 11th Corps in east Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the needs of the transcript, I would just like to note that the witness circled the corps names -- numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the term topographical. So for an army or a country as a whole, what would you say was the main characteristic specific to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you can see right away when you analyse the geographical area is that the eastern area is completely separate and physically remote from the rest of the territory. The western part is elongated and very shallow, looked at from a military perspective in case of action by forces along the line -- the front line between the forces of the Serbian Krajina and the Croatian forces. The depth of the territory or the width of the territory, if you wish, was from 30 to 50 kilometres broad. But when you look from the Dinara Mountains via Benkovac, in this area it was some 80 kilometres broad. All the other area was quite shallow, quite elongated, and exposed to being cut off. What I tried to tell you in the beginning was this: When we were looking at this, we had zone staffs there. And this wasn't something that was set up just like that. The Dalmatia is separated from the Dinara, and that was a border there. So there was also a border between areas of responsibility between Lika and Kordun. There was also a boundary between Kordun and Banija. And Western Slavonia, although there was a physical connection, there was no possibility of actually reaching the area. In order to reach that area, you had to go through Republika Srpska in order to reach Western Slavonia or the area of responsibility of the 18th Corps, which was quite unfavourable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us be precise because of the map. We don't want to be confused later. So let's clarify. The territory controlled by the 39th Corps, in order to reach the area controlled by the 18th Corps, there was no direct access. It did exist physically, but it was not actually used. The way to reach it was through the territory of Republika Srpska. Is this what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a leading question and I object. The witness can say what he wanted to say, not Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm sorry. I just wanted to help, but in a wrong way. And eventually I did something I am not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, could you please explain whether there was any physical connection there; and if not, why.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part that I proximately marked, the territory of Banija and the territory of Western Slavonia join -- are joined on the Sava River, and there is a railway bridge there. There's only a railway bridge there. This bridge was never operational for passenger transport, and the land around it is a marsh land. Therefore, one had to go, as I said, across the territory of Republika Srpska, or rather, under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are still looking at the map, two more things. There is something that we are going to discuss at a later stage, but since the Trial Chamber has the map in front of themselves, I would like to discuss an area which is outside the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina which is called Velika Kladusa. Can you explain where this area was and in what way, if any, was it strategically important for the territory of the Serbian Republic of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, you know, I know that Mr. Harmon seldom stands up to object, but your questions are leading. You are assuming -- you are telling us that Velika Kladusa was of strategic importance. We are not being told by the witness. The way you phrase your question is -- you are actually telling us that that area was of strategic importance, and you are not testifying. The person who is testifying is the witness. You can ask -- frame your question in such a way that you don't tell him that that area was of strategic importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I honestly believe that I didn't make any suggestions to the witness. I asked him whether it was of any strategic importance or not. I can understand in a certain sense that I may have suggested this to the witness, but I really don't believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's read how you have been interpreted: "While we are still looking at the map, two more things. There is something that we are going to discuss at a later stage, but since the Trial Chamber has the map in front of themselves, I would like to discuss an area which is outside the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina which is called Velika Kladusa. Can you explain where this area was and in what way, if any, was it strategically important for the territory of the Serbian Republic of Krajina?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, I wouldn't believe Mr. Lukic if he were to tell me whether this was strategically important or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not important. That's not the point. The point is he mustn't suggest that to you. He must ask you questions and you must tell us, if you do know, whether the area was of strategic importance to you; and if so, why.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is perhaps a discrepancy between the English interpretation of what I said, but as a schoolboy if I put a question whether this was of strategic importance or not, I don't think I can qualify that as a leading question because we are constantly talking about the subject relating to organisation and the functioning of an army. If I put a question of what importance this is, we have to focus on the strategy. And if I ask if this was strategically important or not, I don't believe that's a leading question. At any rate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't believe that was a leading question. I tell you, it is a leading question, Mr. Lukic. And if you can try to avoid asking leading questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to my first question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. After all, you've asked the question anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as a first part of my answer to your question, I will tell you that in the geographical and military assessment made up in the former SFRY, a conclusion was reached that there were several strategic features that were crucial for the whole SFRY - and Mr. Perisic knows well about that. Secondly, the area between Zagreb and Sisak, which is here, including Karlovac and Bihac, was considered to be held by someone to the disadvantage -- to the advantage of them having access to the sea, coastline, and other areas. In our view -- in our view, in the Republic of Serb Krajina, this particular area was exceptionally significant. Our main interest was: If we cannot have friends there, to avoid at least having enemies there. We were anyway outnumbered in the ratio 8:1 in comparison to the Croatian forces. Now, if you add to that an enemy behind our backs with regard to this front line facing the Croatian forces, then that would be a lost cause in advance. This danger was enhanced by the fact that in this area there was a huge number of personnel. There were many young men fit for military service in that area, unlike our area which was demographically very drained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're going to complicate the map too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honours, if in this manner we are going to be able to enter this map into evidence. Do I have to state anything else, or is it possible for you to follow the testimony by way of the transcript? We are going to look at another map anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are in your hands, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we enter the map as it is into evidence and then I will have another copy for more markings to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D436.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, did you want to say something about Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the municipality of Korenica was the least populated one. It had 18 inhabitants per square kilometre. This is just for the sake of comparison with the other areas that we discussed on the Bosnian side of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under which name was this area also known in the map where we see the name "Velika Kladusa"? How was it called apart from that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international community used to call it the Bihac pocket because that was the Bihac protected area, and it was -- also used to be called the autonomous province of Western Bosnia at the time when Mr. Fikret Abdic established such an entity in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we'll still have the map on the screens. I'm going to ask you to make another marking. You mentioned that a minute ago as something that had certain importance to -- for the Army of Republika Krajina. You mentioned the Maslenica bridge. Can you tell us what happened and what the consequences of that attack were as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January of 1993, the Croatian forces launched a massive attack here in the area of the Maslenica strait and in the zone of Ravni Kotari and in the valley of the Cetina towards Knin. Those were the main axes of their attack. There was another attack against Mount Velebit. Perhaps if we enter too many details into this map maybe we should have a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like Your Honours to tender the map as it is into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D437. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretatio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, perhaps you would be sorry to hear that I am reluctant to discuss this conflict any further, but I just wanted to know what the consequence of that attack was with respect to the protected areas according to the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you now told me precisely what you want me to tell you. So the Croatian forces attacked what for the United Nations was Sector South, i.e., an area under the UN protection. In that area, in this particular point that was under the most threat --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's no need for that, General. Let's not dwell on this for too long. Can you just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So a United Nations protected zone was attacked. The UNPROFOR units deployed in that area did not respond in any way whatsoever. They simply vanished from the face of the earth. And these units operated in this area, as they did in any area where there were no UNPROFOR forces, and as a consequence we lost this particular area and never managed to re-capture it. That was basically what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the consequences with regard to this attack concerning your obligations stemming from the Vance Plan? Did you continue to adhere to these obligations?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that morning, we had no other way but to take up arms from the UNPROFOR depot and to defend themselves if UNPROFOR was not prepared to do so. The UNPROFOR units reacted in a variety of ways: Some of them disappeared as an element of the situation prevailing at the time; some of them were in our way because the Croatian forces were operating from their positions; and some UNPROFOR units did help us in an attempt to pull out our heavy artillery to our positions as soon as possible. I can say that openly because I am grateful to those people that this was done by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't hear the name of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters didn't hear the name of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nigerian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, General, or some other representatives of the authorities of the Serbian Krajina have contacts with UNPROFOR and the international community concerning this incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had very intensive contacts with representatives of the international community. I myself didn't have so many of those contacts because I was on the front line. However, representatives of the government and people from the Main Staff in charge of liaising with the international community did have such contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, how did that incident end? Until when did combat go on, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That incident was never fully brought to an end. There was intensive combat in January, February, March. Later on, the intensity of these operations subsided and an agreement was reached to the effect that the Croatian forces should withdraw to their starting positions. I can say that one of the elements involved in this alleviation of the situation was the presidential statement from the United Nations that asked for the same thing. The Croatian forces never fully withdrew from this area. According to that agreement, I think that our milicija was supposed to enter the area; however, they didn't. For me the most important matter in all of this was the fact that the protection force of the UN was not protecting the territory or could not protect the territory. I thought that they would do that not by way of weapons but by way of the authority of the United Nations. Perhaps my thinking was wrong at the time. Perhaps my thinking is wrong to this day. However, it seemed to me then - and I still think so to this day - that Croatia had actually attacked the UN. If that was a UN protected area and if that area was being protected by UN forces, what is this superpower that can attack the United Nations? My understanding, my perception of the situation, was along those lines, and that led me to very pessimistic conclusions in respect of our own destiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us -- could you explain how these pessimistic conclusions of yours were reflected.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to me that foreign political conditions were created in such a way because of the strong international support enjoyed by Croatia at that moment, which was shown by the fact that there was no serious condemnation of what they did on the one hand; and on the other hand, there was the fact that we did not have that kind of international support. Therefore, the balance of power would shift considerably to our detriment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your forecast after March 1993 in terms of whether there could be other attacks against the UNPA, attacks by Croatia, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our assessment was that that was possible. Through our intelligence resources we tried to find out about that, namely, what was the next area that could be in danger, according to this principle of tacit crawling occupation. The situation was as it was in the area, and we were isolated from other parts of the territory that was under our control within the UNPA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, what happened to that heavy weaponry that you took from the depots that had previously been with a double key; were they retained by your forces or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both options were there. In this area that proved to be particularly threatened, that is to say, Northern Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, and Banija, that weaponry remained in their respective firing positions. We could not run the risk of being attacked by Croatian forces and then trying to pull our weapons out of depots. However, in the zone of the 18th Corps in Western Dalmatia and in the area of the eastern part of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, that is to say, in the area of Baranja, Western Srem, and Eastern Slavonia, these weapons and our artillery pieces remained under the double-key principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the representatives of UNPROFOR and the international community in relation to these decisions of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them put that question to me anymore, at least not to me personally, why these weapons of ours were at firing positions. Part of their reaction was that preparations would be underway for a cease-fire. I think that that was their assessment, that that should be done next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago when we discussed the structure of the organisation of the Army of the Serb Republic of Krajina, you showed us what happened before the incident and what the situation was afterwards. In relation to what happened in the Maslenica strait, January 1993, what was the organisation and the structure of the Serb Army of the Krajina like then -- actually, I don't want to go into compound questions yet again.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structure was identical or almost identical, as it was stated in the organisational order. However, the artillery units in the 18th Corps and in the 11th Corps in the eastern part were not fully developed because their weaponry was in UNPROFOR depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to the personnel levels, especially in terms of officers, commissioned and non-commissioned. In that period of time and further on, can you tell us in your assessment what the percentages of personnel levels were for officers in the Serb Republic of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The level was about 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to that first period, the beginning of 1993, in the forthcoming period, were there increases in the number of officers? Let me put a specific question: Did officers of the Army of Yugoslavia come to the Serb Army of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, officers from the Army of Yugoslavia did come to the Serb Army of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, to the best of your recollection, whether there were increases then and what was the level of manning and what was the situation later -- actually, I'm referring to the personnel level in the ranks of the officers of this army.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we could have a very specific questions because there are about two questions or three questions embedded in this. The first question is whether there were increases, what the level of manning was, what the situation was later, et cetera. So if we could have a precise question, it would make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you talked about the percentage of manning in terms of the personnel levels in officers' ranks, 20 per cent. I'm talking about January 1993 onwards. Was that number on the rise; and if so, until when?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number rose over the following two months and then it went down. However, Mr. Lukic, if possible, let us not create any confusion here. When we're talking about officers, commissioned and non-commissioned, of the Serb Army of the Krajina, it's save 5.000 men. Now I don't know whether you are asking me about all of those officers and NCOs of the Serb Army of the Krajina, or are you just asking me about the officers of the former JNA? These are two different things, completely different. Please, if you are asking me about officers and NCOs who are reserve officers who were never members of the JNA but who were officers, commissioned and non-commissioned, of the Serb Army of the Krajina, that is one thing. I can respond as far as they are concerned. Namely, that in January, February, and March, April, for as long as the intensive combat operations were on, that number was at maximum level. However, at the moment when combat operations between our forces and the Croatian forces went down in intensity, the number went down as well. These were people who had their own families, their own problems, and from time to time we had to let them go so that they could provide a living to their own families. As for commissioned and non-commissioned officers of the former Yugoslav army who at that moment had the status of officers of the Army of Yugoslavia as well, likewise their number went down once the intensity of combat was reduced. There wasn't a drastic reduction because individuals from the Army of Yugoslavia agreed to come as if they were tourists on a tour, purportedly waging war for two or three months and then going back. However, from mid-1993 that number was decreased in absolute terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, before the break you gave an answer that relates to the arrival of officers from the Army of Yugoslavia to you, to the Army of the Serbian Krajina. And in the English it was translated as "tourists on tour." You mentioned the term in Serbian, so I don't need to quote it in Serbian. In the following period, were there officers and non-commissioned officers of the JNA who came to the Army of the Serbian Krajina and became officers of the Army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long did they come for? How long were the periods? What was the situation with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would usually come for a period of a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And is that what you said earlier, before the break, as them coming for tourism, as you said on page 26, line 4?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it was a little bit of a picturesque description, but my intention was to say that they came there out of duty, not because they were really motivated to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were there those who came and then stayed until the end of the war or for a longer period of time in the Army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases too. Some of them were killed in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of the members of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, the soldiers and the officers, towards those who would come for brief periods -- towards those who didn't want to stay there for longer?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position was generally not favourable. It was a position of rejection. They were not appreciated, because the people who were at the front from the beginning believed -- thought that their position in terms of the defence of the people was insincere, it wasn't genuine. As far as we were concerned, us in the commands of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, we also had problems because of the -- these people who came. These were usually people of higher rank who mostly sat around in the command, and there was not much use to be had from them. And that's why the commands and the staffs as well lost authority among the fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the command cadre at the level of the battalion. What was the command cadre at the higher level, the command, the corps, in terms of their origin; were they former non-commissioned officers or reserve officers or were they active JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the higher levels of command - brigade, corps level, and the Main Staff level - the cadres were trained JNA officers even though there were some brigade commanders who were reserve officers who were never JNA active officers or active officers of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a number of questions to you now about the financial situation of the Army of the Serbian Krajina for the period from early 1993 until the arrival of General Perisic as Chief of Staff. In terms of the planned organisation of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, what was the situation with weapons in that period, in the period of 1993? And I am thinking about all types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as light infantry weapons are concerned, there was enough of such weaponry. However, a large number of such weapons had already expended their combat resources. That means that a barrel of a rifle is designed to fire a certain number of projectiles. After firing that number of projectiles, the fighter on the front is no longer able to hit his target. As for artillery weapons for support and anti-armour weaponry that are at the level of the battalion and the brigade, there were sufficient such weapons but not enough to provide artillery fire-power to cover the entire front line. And because that line of the front was very long and the weapons when they're placed at the firing positions have a specific area of fire and they can be moved within that area to the left and right but because of their range they need to be close to the front -- so without going into any more detail, let me just say that the number of the artillery batteries for support was insufficient to be able to provide fire support for all the sections of the front. As far as artillery support -- missile and rocket weaponry for support is concerned, there were plenty of these weapons because these weapons can quickly change their positions. As for armoured combat vehicles, it was our estimate that we did have a sufficient number of them, but they also had expended their combat resources and were already in the stage that because they had already fired a specific number of projectiles and the engine had been working for a specific number of hours they needed maintenance. And so because of all these things, as we saw before, I would always ask - and we never had enough of those, and these were actually the transport vehicles -- modern warfare had indicated that armoured units, in case of need, would have to be transferred 200, 300 kilometres further along; and for that we needed vehicles in order to be able to move the weaponry. So we were not able to do this because there was a shortage of these vehicles. As for anti-aircraft fire, we lacked artillery and rocket systems in a sufficient number to be able to defend the skies above our territory. As for planes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the PVO system? When you're saying "in order to defend our skies," are you thinking about the PVO systems?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the PVO systems, anti-aircraft defence systems, yes. As for planes, their number was also reduced to just a few fighter bombers. And planes that would be able to deal with other fighter planes attacking our territory, we didn't actually have any of those planes. This is a brief description of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question: All these items that you said that you had, how did you acquire them? Was that something that you already had? Was it given to you from -- by somebody? Did you procure them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. The question that was asked is: How did you acquire them? That is sufficient. Mr. Lukic is now suggesting a number of possibilities, and I think it's up to the witness to answer the first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the objection. I'm going to rephrase my question if I did create a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So how did the Army of the Serbian Krajina obtain all of these weapons? How did it come to have them?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to this question, I can state only what is true. And the truth is that this was weaponry that had remained after or behind the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation with ammunition in that period, in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ammunition expenditure was enormous, and this was so on all sides. In war we always had a problem with ammunition. The least problem was rifle ammunition, and this is where we could count on the help of the Army of Yugoslavia. But as far as artillery ammunition, tank projectiles, rockets were concerned, that was always a major problem, and we never had enough of such ammunition. In answering this question, I also have to say that the Republic of the Serbian Krajina did not have its own facilities for the production of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation in the beginning? I would like to know. And later? Perhaps I didn't get a precise answer about that regarding ammunition. Was there enough ammunition from the beginning, or was this shortage something that occurred right from the start?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, there was enough ammunition. But during intense combat, during the Croatian offensive around the Maslenica inlet and the Ravni Kotari and the Cetina River valley and Mount Velebit, ammunition was spent very intensively, and then we were in a situation when we had insufficient amounts of the types of ammunition that I had spoken about before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbian army of the Krajina have an established system of communications?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how this was set up, based on what?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications system of the Army of the Serbian Krajina was set up using means of communication, the communication facilities which had remained behind after the Yugoslav People's Army. Operators of those communications devices were members of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, i.e., there was a small number of professional officers from the Yugoslav People's Army and later the Army of Yugoslavia; and the majority of others were from the reserve force who were trained in their capacity as non-commissioned officers, officers, and reserve officers in the JNA to use these communications devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, In an army, what should this signals or communications system be like?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All military documents state that the communications system should be such as to satisfy the requirements of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did this system of communications satisfy the requirements of command that you were using on the basis of this infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This system of communications in essence did make command activities possible. However, it was not at the level required. And if you would like me to, I can explain why it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the principles of the tactics of the signals or communication service, it has to be such a system as to meet the requirements of command. The first one is that it should be uninterrupted. The system of communications should be such that in the event of enemy action when one source of communication is cut off, one type of communication is interrupted, another kind of communication is activated. And the communications for command and other types of communication continue to work without interruption. Because of a limited number of resources that we had, this principle could not be secured. And later this became evident in combat. Then there has to be a sufficient number of protected channels of communication. We found a small number of encryption communication devices in order to be able to have secure communications only for some basic communications channels that were covering the command. Then the system has to be such that it is protected from radio surveillance, what in these documents is being treated as an intercepted conversation. Because of a small number of communication devices for such type of communication, we were unable to have this facility at the required level. So these would be the main things. I don't need to go into this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the period when you were a commander and later, are you aware if the Army of the Serbian Krajina kept perfecting this system that it had available from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I -- that we were relying on existing devices and facilities that were previously used by the Yugoslav People's Army in that area. However, our requirements and the deployment of our units and our commands was quite different from that one of the Yugoslav People's Army in that area. The command before the war, the command of the north-western theatre of operations that commanded the bulk of the forces in Croatia, Slovenia, and a part of Bosnia, was located in Zagreb. Of course, all those communications lines were then directed at that area and also connected to the General Staff that was located in Belgrade. So, now, what did we have to do? These communications facilities with those devices for the operative levels of communication were something that we now took; let's say there was a facility in Petrova Gora and there were many other radio nodes. For example, there were 25 devices, 15 directed towards Belgrade, 15 directed towards Zagreb. We would then have to connect those devices to antennas that were facing our corps commands, let's say 95 per cent of them. And then 5 per cent of those devices or even less would still be turned towards the areas controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska and which could then, if needed, be used and directed for communications with Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the system function independently?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did function completely independently for our purposes, for communications in our area, that is to say, with the eastern part, the 11th Corps in Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem, and then you had to actually go through the territory of Republika Srpska, or rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As a matter of fact, I think that you didn't have to go through the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. From Mount Majevica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down. The interpreter is struggling to keep pace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I seem to be carried away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a technical detail. I cannot say right now whether our communications channel vis-à-vis the 11th Corps went from Mount Majevica. I think it was that way according to the schematic in Eastern Bosnia and Semberija straight towards our 11th Corps. Technically that would have been fine. Or it went via Mount Avala, the node near Belgrade. I think it was the first variant, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No problem whatsoever. General, after you became commander of the Serb Republic of the Krajina, did you establish contact with the commanders of some other armies?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But not with all immediately. I established contact with the Chief of Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia General Panic. I did not see General Mladic - I know that very well - up until the summer or spring, spring or the beginning of the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a general picture as to how often you saw General Panic while he was Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was perhaps once or twice during 1992, then -- actually, up until mid-January 1993 when the Croatian offensive started in Northern Dalmatia. Then I did not see him for at least two months. After that, while he still held that position, it was at least once or twice a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Briefly, what was the objective of these meetings with General Panic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I wished to inform the then-Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia directly about the elements involved in our assessment of the situation in our area. Secondly, it was my effort to resolve the basic problems I had in the army. The way we understood things, the main problems were of a materiel nature and personnel nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In simple words, did you ask him for some help?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask for help. First of all, I asked for assistance in terms of officers. I saw that the level of training of the reserve commissioned and non-commissioned officers was insufficient if you look at the requirements of modern technology and equipment. Through my officers in the Krajina who were in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time, I received a computer list with the names and surnames of -- age included, type of professional training of officers and NCOs, and the garrisons where they were serving in the Army of Yugoslavia. It was about 6.000 names all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You said that your officers gave it to you. They were originally from Krajina, right, these 6.000 that you referred to? Are they all officers of the Army of Yugoslavia or are they your group?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they were natives of the Krajina, but they were officers of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I was asking about in more specific terms. So originally they came from where?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of their place of birth, they came from the Krajina; however, at that moment they were serving in different garrisons in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please go on. What did you do with this computer list once you received it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with my associates, I compiled a list -- we compiled a list, trying primarily to get people who would change the quality of our units, that is to say, people for command positions; say platoon commanders, company commanders, battalion commanders, even brigade commanders, even corps commanders. That was a very specific list, including specific names. I took that list and went to see General Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened at General Panic's in relation to that list?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Panic said that if he were to give me these 750 men in total that I had asked for that he might as well disband the Army of Yugoslavia. That was his interpretation. The explanation was that these people headed the best-trained units that the Army of Yugoslavia had. However, I was not satisfied with that answer of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at a document first. Prosecution Exhibit P1132.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it is in the context of what you're testifying about now. This is a document that you signed; isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The date is the 20th of June, 1993. Who was Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the document, and I would just like to ask you for a brief comment in relation to that document.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I had asked for 750 officers for command positions, at that. Now, you can see here that it says that what had been agreed upon was to send 300 officers and non-commissioned officers. I don't know -- if necessary, I can explain how that happened that I asked for 750 and that ultimately it was decided it would be 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was dissatisfied with General Panic's answer when he said that he might as well disband the army if he were to give me these 750 commissioned and non-commissioned officers, I went to see President Milosevic with the very same request. He organised a meeting then between General Panic and myself in his presence. Now, that looked like bargaining to me. I presented my arguments; General Panic presented his arguments why he could not give me this personnel; I saw that I did not really have much support from Mr. Milosevic; and then the agreement was that it would be 300 commissioned and non-commissioned officers, however, those that were essential to me for the quality of command and control. You see here, on the 20th of June I state on the basis of reports and records in the Main Staff of the Serb Army of the Krajina that instead of the 750 agreed upon, it was -- or rather, 300 officers agreed upon, only 78 had arrived ultimately. I got officers, commissioned and non-commissioned, who belonged to the navy and technical services. We had no navy at the time. I got an expert for computers, and thereby I was in a position to establish a computer centre that would have been at European level. I got a pharmacist and I did not have a pharmaceutical industry at all; we don't have one in the territory of the Serb Krajina. I also got a few commissioned and non-commissioned officers from the air force and its technical service, and I didn't really need them either. Now, that is the reason why I am going back to what I had asked for in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, a question that stems from your answer, and I believe that the others in court will be interested in that: Why did you address President Milosevic after that first conversation with Panic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because it was generally known that he was the main political authority in Serbia and in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. If he could not resolve that, then there was no one who could have resolved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now look at another document, and we'll discuss these personnel issues later as well. However, I would like to deal with the general subject now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1617, could we have that on our screens now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia from February 1993. Again, I'm going to ask you who the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia was at the time, although I believe that the question is superfluous now.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. General Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what do you know in relation to this document? As we can see, it was sent to you as well, that is to say, to your Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see that this document is being sent by the operations centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. That means that that is the kind of organisational unit that any army has. It follows the situation on a daily basis, both on the territory of its own state and the territory in the surrounding area and even beyond that. As regards armed forces and their activities that are of interest for that particular army. In this particular case, information is requested about the most important activities in the areas engulfed by war. This is the area that this administration believes it should follow and record on a daily basis what was going on there; they should record it in their own operations centre. You see, that's what they say here themselves: To facilitate timely and more complete information, the assessment of and the monitoring of -- it is the paragraph above item number 1. They say please. In military terms, there is a clear distinction. They are asking us to inform them, not to report to them. They cannot issue an order like that to us. If you look at the activities that followed after this document, that would probably be of interest, then you would see how things developed in relation to this request of theirs. I think that this is a normal, professional attempt to follow the situation in the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This information that is being requested specifically from numbers 1 through 4, why do you think that they are important for the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia? Why do they need to know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because these are elements that are the basic elements of the situation as it is. You can see that here. You can see here the composition, deployment, and strength of the enemy and probably the directions in which their activity could take place and also on our side what it is that we intend to do and whether there is anything else. Basically, they want to have insight into the situation in the war zone. What was selected here was selected for that reason, because these are elements that are essential for assessing the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And why was it important for them to have this insight?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important because the operations centre must monitor the situation in the surrounding areas. For the requirements of command of the VJ, there is no such centre that can afford to be such a laid-back institution and fail to follow the situation. There is no such centre in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember back in February 1993 and this request, did you provide them with this information that they asked for?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that for a certain period of time we did provide this information; however, the Main Staff was extremely understaffed and the existing members of the Main Staff worked around the clock. Quite simply, we were unable and we didn't have the capacity to do whatever was not a top priority in the operation of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago when you asked about the purpose of your meeting with General Panic, you highlighted two problems: personnel and financial resources. We talked about the personnel. Let's move now to this second topic. Did you ask General Panic for resources to replenish the Serbian Army of Krajina, and what was the situation in that sphere?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, our main concern was ammunition. And I know that I asked General Panic to try and solve at least some of our problems. I believe that we did receive a certain amount of ammunition from General Panic at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 65 ter document of the Defence 01006-D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at this document. And it says here that it was drafted by you. Can you please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina issued to the command of the 18th and 11th Corps of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina asking them or requesting them to participate in carrying out certain obligations with regard to making a solemn pledge. That was a procedure that had been applied previously by the JNA. However, in the Serbian Army of Krajina we now had a different wording of the pledge to be given by the troops from the one that had been in use by the Yugoslav Army at the time. According to the protocol for such occasions that we ourselves set up at the Main Staff of Krajina, this ceremony was participated by a priest as well, and the wording ended with the phrase "so help me God." Therefore, it was a different phrasing that was used by the VJ, and the protocol itself was different. That is why the corps command were obligated in this respect to make sure that these recruits make this solemn pledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. When you say that these recruits were there, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, it says "Subotica." It says on the occasion of taking a solemn oath in Subotica. We are talking about April 1993 and the personnel of the RSK. So first tell me where Subotica is, and why is it written in this way in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subotica was a VJ garrison situated in the far north of Serbia, close to the Hungarian border. This is where at the time an armoured brigade of the VJ was deployed. According to an agreement with the General Staff of the VJ, we sent recruits for training to the Subotica garrisons for such military specialties for which we in the Republic of Serbian Krajina did not have conditions to provide training for. As far as I can remember, those were such duties that were carried out by tank crews or by anti-armour launch-rocket weapon operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why was it important for you that those recruits take this solemn pledge there according to the rules of the Serbian Army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, I find this question a little bit odd. Whose else solemn pledge would they take other than the one that was in force in the Serbian Army of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am satisfied with your answer, although you're not happy with my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D438. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this same subject, can we have a Prosecution exhibit, P940, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is now February 1994. You are still the commander of the Serbian Army of Krajina. Can you briefly comment on this document, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is again to do with making a solemn oath by the recruits in the Army of Yugoslavia. However, here we are informing the General Staff and the office of the Chief of the General Staff of VJ that for this ceremony of giving a solemn pledge we were going to drive these recruits and soldiers to the territory of the Serbian Republic of Krajina to the village of Vojnic in Kordun and that that would be the place where they would take their solemn oath. Therefore, there was no question raised again about whether co-operation was going to be good, whether somebody else should be helping us with this. We took full responsibility for this ceremony of giving a solemn pledge, of course with allowing for a possibility, as the tradition goes, for this ceremony to be attended by family members and friends as well as the tradition in the former Yugoslav People's Army. Because this kind of ceremony had always been a solemn one and always attended by family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention in the transcript. Probably there is some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads here that you stated that this again refers to giving a solemn oath by the recruits in the Yugoslav Army. I suppose that's not what you said, so can you please be more specific. Whose recruits are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If necessary, we can read the document. But it is obvious that this refers to the recruits of the Serbian Army of Krajina who at this juncture when this order was being written --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's clear now. That was all we wanted to clarify. General, one question relating to this topic and the stay of these recruits from the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the Army of Yugoslavia and their training there. What kind of information did you receive as a feedback regarding their relationship with members of the VJ [sic] and officers of the VJ at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information we received indicated that there were problems in that area. There were conflicts between the trainees and the VJ officers who were instructors. To put it simply, they did not want to recognise them as their own officers. They did not wear the same insignia on their caps. They did not believe to be, themselves, part of one and the same army, and therefore they could not be commanded by members of another army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. I guess you might need an intervention again here at page 44, line 23: "... relationship with members of the VJ and ..." -- "... members of the SVK and officers of the VJ ..." I think is what you wanted to say. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I expanded my question and I put my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
