utterances.text: That's the answer -- look at line 23. It says "members of the VJ and officers of the VJ at the time." Is it not supposed to be members of the SVK and officers of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's right. You're absolutely right. So on page 44, line 23, I asked about the relationship between the recruits from the Serbian Army of Krajina who were undergoing training there, and I thank Your Honour for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, let's move to another topic now. I'm interested now in your contacts with General Perisic starting from August 1993. We have information that General Perisic was appointed to the position of the Chief of General Staff of the VJ. Can you remember when you first met him in your capacity, and can you recall anything about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot give you the exact date, but I do know that it might have taken place some ten days after he had been appointed to that post. I wanted to meet Mr. Perisic because from our previous meetings I got the impression that he was a smart man and a capable officer and my expectations were that he would demonstrate at least some professional understanding of the situation in which the army of which I was the commander found itself. During this first meeting that we had, I informed him about the basic elements pertaining to the situation. This was done more or less on the principle of the document that was shown here in which the operations centre of the General Staff asked information from us about four subjects or items. So those were basically these elements of the situation relating to the enemy and what was known about the situation relating to our forces about what we thought we could and should do in the forthcoming period and about the influence of the external factors involved in the situation, starting from UNPROFOR to those at the political and diplomatic levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you speak about the topics that you discussed with General Panic -- if not then, when was the first time that you discussed those topics? This is your cadre problem and the problem of the financial situation with the army.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about that as well, of course, because that was part of that item 2 that was on the document, own forces. If you want, I can tell you what I told General Perisic about the situation of our own forces, the forces of the Army of the Serbian Krajina. I began by describing its strategic position, operations position at certain sectors of the front, combat morale, and the situation with materiel and equipment, logistics, including also the medical aspect of it. I did this to the extent that I believed necessary at the level of the Chief of the General Staff, which was the position of General Perisic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion or later, did you ask him for assistance? I'm primarily thinking about materiel, equipment, and so on. What was his position about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Just as was the case with General Panic before him, I asked for material assistance from him, personnel, and also in certain kinds of materiel and equipment. I felt that General Perisic understood the situation in terms of these being realistic requirements. Unfortunately, however, I did not encounter - and I can begin like that and I can end in the same way as well - his actual ability to resolve these problems, either the materiel and equipment or the personnel matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what he specifically told you about the request for funds or material assistance?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we knew each other from before, at one point he opened his cash box, his safe, that was in his office, and it was full of -- it was full of secrets, just like the ones that we're looking at now. And he said, Here, take a look for yourself. And the things that General Perisic showed me then, it was enough to make a grown man cry - I mean we could put it like that in Serbian. That Army of Yugoslavia and in relation to the things that I needed the most, ammunition was in a very, very sorry state indeed. If you have a tank, for example, and the -- a tank -- each tank has to have 50 projectiles, 50 shells. This is part of the combat kit. It's a requirement. And then you have three times as much in a brigade and then seven times as much up to the level of the Supreme Command. This means that a regular army would require 4- or 500 projectiles per tank. And what the Army of Yugoslavia had at the time was just enough to supply the requirements of -- at the level of a unit. This was from 100 to 150 projectiles [as interpreted]. If we're talking about rockets; for example, each launcher should have six rockets. I remember that the best for anti-armour rockets. I can still see that number now. A combat kit is six rockets. At that point in time, he had 0.3 of that combat kit. That means less than two rockets per projectile.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Before, it was supposed to be "from 150 to 180 projectiles."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. What you have just said now -- I apologise to the interpreters. What was your conclusion, General, from this information that you were able to find out, read, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible to draw a number of conclusions; the main one being that the Army of Yugoslavia really without endangering the basic purpose for its existence could not provide us with ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question and then we'll go on a break. We don't have to discuss this very first meeting, this specific meeting. But on the basis of your meetings with General Perisic, what was the conclusion you drew -- actually, we heard yesterday that the Yugoslav People's Army took an active part in the combat; you said that yesterday. What was his position in relation to any kind of active participation of the Yugoslav Army in the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We absolutely did not discuss that during that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about subsequent conversation; did you get the impression that he had some sort of position in relation to that matter?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what he said, you could draw the conclusion -- I mean, you could draw the conclusion - I don't think he could have said it openly at the time - the Army of Yugoslavia did not have the basic prerequisites for waging war. And this did not apply only to the materiel situation either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suggest that we go on our second break for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us whether in the autumn of 1993 there were some new incidents in the territory of the Republic of the Serb Krajina; and if so, where and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of September 1993, the Croatian forces attacked a zone in Lika, which was later known as the Medak pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's be practical. While you continue speaking, let us have D164 on the screen, that's a map, so that we have it there while you're speaking.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an area that is between the very high mountain of Velebit and the town of Gospic, which was under Croatian control. That area, I mean the part of the area that was under our control, was in the shape of a triangle vis-à-vis the area that was held by Croatian forces, and it was below a part of Mount Velebit that was held by the Croatian forces. Visocica is the elevation there where, according to our information, there was the staff or headquarters of the special Croatian police. If necessary, I can indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the General actually mark that, could he mark that area on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please go on.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian forces started grouping their forces for this attack a few days in advance. There was a strong unit of the Croatian special police that our intelligence people discovered as they were moving from their headquarters in Zagreb, and we knew that this group was headed towards the area of Lika. However, we did not know specifically which part of the front they were heading to. Also, they discovered some unusual activity on their part on Mount Velebit --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The question that was asked is essentially to tell us what happened, and we are going into extraordinary detail that I think is unnecessary for purposes of the question that was asked by Mr. Lukic. So I would ask the Court to instruct the witness to answer the question that he was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will accept the objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because, General, we have a great many topics that we have to discuss that are quite important for this trial, I believe that you would like to tell us a lot about this action and you could indeed, however, I would like you to focus and to be as specific as possible. In your view, what was the objective of this operation? Please give us the briefest possible answer, and let's move on to other topics.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear. It's unequivocal. And I can give further explanation if necessary, but I don't really think it's needed. The only objective of this Croatian operation was to demonstrate to us, Serbs, the method of scorched earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you trying -- could you please tell us what "scorched earth" means?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this exemplary example, as it were, this exemplary case, the scorched earth method means kill all living creatures, persons and animals included, in a given area and destroy everything that was created by human hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear this term from, scorched earth?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this term several times earlier on in different -- on different occasions, but in this particular case I heard this term from General Jean Cot, UNPROFOR commander. He's the one who used the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On which occasion did he use that term?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he first met me, after he personally toured the area. General Cot was an officer who wanted to see this personally and indeed he did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it that he conveyed to you then, which information did he come across on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to be as brief as possible again. General Cot stated in the briefest possible terms that he was totally astounded by what he had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In view of the position that you had then as the commander of the Army of the Serb Krajina, did you see General Cot again, and did you see any representatives of the international community in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw General Cot several times in relation to this incident. As far as I can remember, General Bo Pellnas was always with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see now that what the general drew simply disappeared. Would that be right? Oh no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry, I made a mistake. This is a technical problem. Could you please draw the area of the Medak pocket again on this map.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, General, is this territory strategically important for the Croatian army, the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. As a matter of fact, it's not even important from the point of view of the explanation that the Croats, the official Croatian authorities, gave, namely, that that was their response to the shelling of Gospic. If you look at this part of the front line that is jutting out, as it were, there was nothing of the kind. They could see that from the dominant elevations that they held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please admit this into evidence now, Your Honours, before we actually lose this image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D439. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this attack halted? Did it stop in any way? What happened after that aggression?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack of the Croatian forces was stopped at the line of the village of Medak and the road that goes through the village of Medak. This is a continuation of this straight line from Gospic and then further down south. That is to say that they only entered this area that is jutting out; however, operations continued nevertheless. General Cot and, as far as I know, the international representatives in Zagreb tried to reach some kind of agreement in order to end the hostilities. I was told that the Croatian side is refusing to discuss anything with anyone from the international community with regard to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who said that to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told by General Cot and General Pellnas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time, as for those who were withdrawing from the area, I heard the same thing from them that I heard from General Pellnas, namely, that the civilian population was being massacred and that all living creatures were being destroyed in the said area. Because of that, I decided to threaten the Croatian side in order to force them to stop doing such terrible things. For a few days, all the media that were under our control stated publicly and persistently repeated the list of military objectives in the territory of Croatia - I repeat - exclusively military targets that would be targeted by the Serb side unless what is happening in the area that they had taken is brought to a halt. At the same time, the civilian population was asked to move away from these military objectives. These military objectives or targets were exclusively of a military nature, namely, the basis of the special Croatian police that we knew was participating in this action, the bases and the command posts of the Croatian army. After there was no change in the situation, as a matter of fact, their activity continued unabated, we did target some military facilities of this kind. The first facility that we targeted was the base of the special police at the former airfield with a grass runway, Lucko it was called. It is to the west of Zagreb. Further on, it was the barracks in Jastrebarsko which is between Zagreb and Karlovac. I think that that was the barracks of the communications unit of the Croatian Main Staff in the Samo barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were there any civilian casualties during these attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any reports stating that there were civilian casualties sustained during these attacks. This base of the special police in Lucko that is outside built-up areas, it was not hit. Also, the barracks in Jastrebarsko were not hit, and the town of Jastrebarsko wasn't hit either. This Luna rocket fell closer to the highway, fell onto an empty space there. That is what I know about these targets of ours and civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want the transcript to reflect this: What were the rockets that you used for carrying out these operations?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the firing positions were being changed at the time, we temporarily had a battery of Luna M -- or, rather, R-65 missiles. According to the NATO marking, it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] FROG-7. Frog, as in the animal, frog.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, and what was the reaction, if there was any, of the UNPROFOR to this action of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shortly afterwards, General Cot reported that the Croats had agreed, the Croatian authorities, President Tudjman primarily and the chief of their Main Staff General Bobetko, agreed to speak with them. General Pellnas told me that he was glad - I repeat - that he was glad when he heard that our FROG was flying towards Belgrade -- towards Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Towards Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because up until then, they were completely ignored in their requests to be received by both the Croatian civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to this incident, what was the impression this incident made on you - I asked you this about Maslenica earlier - in terms of further possible attacks against the Krajina and the position of the Croatian authorities on that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our assessment that the Croatian side would continue with merciless armed actions in order to establish complete control over the territory and areas under the protection of the UN, namely, the territory of Republika Srpska. The second conclusion was that the population in the territory under our control was of no interest to them; rather, they were interested in an empty territory only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We're going to move to a different topic now. In preparations for this testimony, I was able to show you some documents that we referred to as the notebooks or notes of General Mladic in the courtroom. My question was: Did I show you any documents like that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in view of the decision of the Trial Chamber we can remain in public session, and I would like to go through some of these documents from batch 410 with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, these documents, did they refresh your recollection about some event and meetings that you had?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first document that I would like to look at with the General is a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honour, we are going to follow this procedure that we had earlier, and that is primarily I'm going to ask the -- your agreement to introduce into our 65 ter list of exhibits of the Defence this document, that is, a document that I'm marking with the mark 65 ter 03382D, which in the B/C/S starts from 0668-2627 - that is the ERN page - until 2637 -- actually, in the e-court it goes up to 2640. This is notes from a meeting with President Milosevic of the 24th of September, 1993. So let me first hear the position of the Prosecution before we are able to use the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection to this document being added to the Defence 65 ter list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic, it's so added.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I start going through the document with the witness - and there will be a number of them - I just wanted to inform the Trial Chamber that what you see before you is an official translation we received from the translation service. However, when we were going through the document of this official translation, we encountered certain translations which we find are inadequate. Some of them are not so important, but there are a few that we do consider important. I've informed Mr. Harmon about it, and I marked the parts which we believe are in dispute, and his suggestion was to ask the translation service to retranslate this document and then we can tender this new translation into evidence. So when I'm going through the documents with the witness, I'm going to ask the witness to read certain parts or I can read them and the witness can confirm that that is what is said in the translation. We have also provided copies to the interpreters in the booths. And we have marked those parts that we believe are inaccurate, and we've asked them to pay special attention to those parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic and his team provided me with copies of these documents and the portions that they assert need to be retranslated. I've looked at them with my language assistants. I agree with some of the suggestions; I don't agree with other suggestions. When matters are read into the record, I would like to make it perfectly clear that I -- on disputed areas, I'm not accepting the - with all deference to the language booth - the interpreter's reading as the correct and definitive translation. I think if these are submitted to CLSS, these portions that are in dispute, that we should be guided by CLSS's translation of these and not the oral reading and the quick interpretation of what's on these documents. So insofar as the procedure that Mr. Lukic has identified, if he will identify those portions to where we have a dispute, and then we can have CLSS regulate that matter for us as the official document that would be guiding the Court and the parties in their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that acceptable to you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That is what I said. That can be a final version. We can send it to the translation section, and then their version would be the final one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Okay. You may proceed then. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we see in front of us the first page of several that will follow, and it says: "Meeting with President Milosevic" of the 24th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, the 24th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, the 24th of September, 1993. We're going to go page by page. But what we see from the document is that the participants in this conversation are General Perisic, General Mladic -- actually, this is General Mladic's notebook so I'm drawing the conclusion on the basis of that. And you are also mentioned. So I'm just asking you if you remember that this meeting was held at that time in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you perhaps recall whether, other than those persons mentioned as being present here, anyone else was present also, or were they only the persons that are actually referred to that attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the meeting was only between the persons that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're now going to go section by section, and I will ask you to comment based on your recollection of that conversation whether what is written down here adequately reflects what that person, that participant, said in the conversation. General Perisic is mentioned first. I am not going to read the first two sentences. Are you able to read, or should I read?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this reflect General Perisic's words adequately? According to your recollection, is that what he said at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my best recollection, it does absolutely reflect what was said because that was what his assessments -- that's what his assessments were and his view about the situation. I especially want to mention the third point; they are very strong, logistical support, logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is where my first remark was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Your Honours, in the English version and the B/C/S version, this is my objection to the translation service: They're placing something in parenthesis, interpreting what is being written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, please, what it says here is: "They are very strong PO." What does that mean? What do you think that means?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the standard abbreviations used by General Mladic, and they were commonly used in the schools that we completed, this can only mean the term that we used and that is "logistics support." "Pozadinsko obezbedjenje." This is a term that is practically identical to the term "logistics." It's not entirely the same, "pozadinsko obezbedjenje," "rear support," but more or less those two terms mean the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. When he says "they," who did he refer to, General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant Croatia, which he mentions immediately before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the incident that we mentioned before, when we look at the date here, can you please tell us the date of the Medak incident in relation to this meeting here?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident began on the 9th of September, and this is the period immediately after General Stipetic and I signed some kind of an agreement on the cessation of hostilities, and the Canadian Battalion from UNPROFOR pushed the Croatians out of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm going to read the next paragraph, and you can just confirm to me whether I've read it adequately because of the translation. "Help in manpower (senior officers) everything is on a voluntary basis ... to go for a more radical position, that everyone who was born there should go."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm particularly reading the following sentence because of the translation, Your Honours. "To persuade them as much as we can to go there." For example, if I can comment now. I'm quite satisfied with the translation from the booth, but in any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No. I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic may be satisfied with the translation from the booth. This is a portion that we have an issue with, and this is the area where I think we should be guided by the official CLSS translation and not the translation from the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you say so, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I just commented. I just wanted to draw your attention to what it was that we saw as the discrepancy between the official translation and what we were pointing to. We don't want to go into details or we don't want to burden the translation service in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We will send --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, did I read this correctly, what I have just read to you? And I'm going to ask you, Can you please confirm?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your comment on the position of General Perisic in relation to the departure of officers and which officers. What does this exactly refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Lukic. Doesn't the document speak for itself on that point, provided that we get a correct translation from CLSS?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand you very well now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I have a problem with your question. You're saying: "Can you give us your comment on the position of General Perisic in relation to the departure of officers and which officers. What does this exactly refer to." Now, there is a minute here written by General Mladic about which there is a dispute between the parties on the interpretation. Okay? We are going to get CLSS to re-look at that translation and tell us whether they stand by what's written here or whether they are prepared to change. And once we've got that, that will be the position of General Perisic, which the witness's comment on that position doesn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I have to give you my comment. When we get this translation, that will be a position being recorded in this document as being the position of General Perisic. So what I'm going to ask Mr. Novakovic is, Does he recollect that, or What does he recollect was General Perisic's position on the basis of this document on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not asking for a comment; you're asking for his recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The first question was "comment."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we've understood each other. Yes, you can go ahead and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your recollection, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, your recollection, Mr. Novakovic, sorry. Forget about the entry. What is your recollection of General Perisic's position on the departure of officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all I wanted to say is that this reminds me of the position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that you remember the position -- [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because if I were honest, I really couldn't say whether that was the position or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand perfectly. Now that you remember, tell us, What is your recollection of that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gist of the position of General Perisic on this matter on sending officers and non-commissioned officers who were born in our area who were at that time in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was that he didn't have a legal basis to send them there, that the dispatch up until that moment was on the principle of voluntarity, voluntariness, and that it did not depend on him, basically whether those people would go there or not. And that was the practice as well at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the next page. We're still dealing with the words of General Perisic. Now I would like to comment on the second and third sentence. "Issuing OB equipment (weapons, ammunition, fuel) ..." What does the abbreviation "OB" mean? Do you recall what it was that Perisic was saying in respect of this entry?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's two questions. The first is: What does the abbreviation OB mean? That's the first question. The second question is: Do you recall what he was saying in respect of this entry. So if we could have the answer to the first question, we could proceed to the second question. But I object because the question is compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that that question was that complex that the witness cannot be in a position to answer it. In order to speed things up --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, General, what do you believe "OB" means?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me - and General Perisic completed the same school that I did - OB means "organ bezbednosti," "security organ." However, what I find illogical is how come it is followed by "weapons, ammunition, fuel." So at this point in time I cannot confirm anything. I cannot remember now what this exactly pertained to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next entry that says: "Regulating the status of officers (from retirement issues to purchasing uniforms) ..." Does this jog your memory in any way in terms of the words of General Perisic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an answer to our constant requests to resolve the questions of the status of professional officers who are still being registered as serving in the Army of Yugoslavia but are actually in the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serb Army of the Krajina. Status-related questions are not resolved for them as they are for those professional military personnel who are serving in the garrisons of the Army of Yugoslavia, starting with the matter of not having their years of service recorded properly, therefore they do not have the necessary number of years of service as the administration personnel put it but they actually do have a sufficient number of service. Then also their medical insurance for them and for their family members so that they can receive medical treatment in military medical institutions. Then the basic problem, the very ordinary problem of purchasing uniforms. I was glad at that point in time to see General Perisic stating these problems for starters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your problem in terms of medical services being provided and uniforms being purchased? I'm referring to the Army of Yugoslavia now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, this witness was in the Army of the Serbian Krajina. Would he know the problems within the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking him about his problem as an officer of the SVK. How did he get medical treatment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- look at line 18 there, page 66: "I'm referring to the Army of Yugoslavia now." And that is preceded by a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- which was: "What was your problem in terms of medical services being provided and uniforms being purchased?" Now, his problem is a problem of the SVK, not of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I'm going to rephrase the question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, as a member of the SVK, could you purchase uniforms from the depots of the Army of Yugoslavia just like officers of the Army of Yugoslavia could?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the problem?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was because in my military ID there was not a military post code number or a military unit number from the Army of Yugoslavia. If I have that kind of number in my military ID, I could have purchased a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the problem with the medical insurance cards that you had for using medical services of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military medical insurance card of a military medical insuree of -- that is to say, of a military officer of the Army of Yugoslavia and family members of such military personnel who had the same rights on the basis of that person's employment with the Army of Yugoslavia, namely, to be treated in military medical hospitals, that depended at the time and depends to this day in Serbia on the following: Whether the medical insurance card has been stamped, whether it has been verified, by way of a stamp, that the military insuree is serving in a specific military post in the Army of Yugoslavia, that is on the list of the military post of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now the next entry; does that jog your memory? What were these words that were uttered by General Perisic? It says: "Material financial support."

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a continuation -- I mean this notebook is not stenographic notes. I remember this part. It's not that I don't remember it. General Perisic was talking about insufficient material financial support. First of all, the Army of Yugoslavia didn't have that, and he said that that was the main reason why he cannot meet our requests for material resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now an entry that pertains to you, so I'll just ask you what this means, what it says here, "min snage vojin." Do you remember what this means? Could you tell us briefly what the term "vojin" is?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have an excellent recollection of that because that was a big problem for me. This correctly reflects what I had asked for. It means minimal forces for air surveillance, reporting, and guidance. Minimum forces for air surveillance, reporting, and guidance. That is a system that controls the situation in the air-space. That exists in every army of the world, that is to say, above one's territory and on the approaches to your territory by way of radar, visual equipment, and other equipment; you monitor and observe everything that is in the air-space. You identify enemy targets. And also what it says here at the end, "guiding," as for your own anti-aircraft equipment, you guide it so as to destroy enemy targets. Also, a clear distinction is being made here in terms of identifications, what is an enemy target, and what are other aircraft in the air-space.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, at the time, did the SVK have a developed "vojin" system?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. At the time, we did not have a developed "vojin" system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Up until the end of the war, did you manage to develop a "vojin" system?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We never managed to develop a "vojin" system for our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. I don't have to read. Could you just give me your comment about the next entries. What is the meaning of what you were saying then?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next entry has to do with air-space control above our territory. Because if your observation system detects an enemy target in the air-space and if you do not have an air force to down such aircraft, well then you don't really need observation equipment in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on a bit faster. We had a bit of a problem here. Can you explain to us this so that the translators can translate it there. It says here at the end: "Six heavy-duty haulage vehicles to transport T." Do you remember what "T" meant at the time? We have a problem with the translation there. Could you just tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of my remarks today, I mentioned to this -- I mentioned this problem of towing vehicles. These are vehicles that have a platform for loading tanks. So "T" means "tanks" in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The translation service correctly interpreted this in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, the entry says that this is what you had said. So could you give us your comments, briefly. To the best of your recollection, what was it that you were talking about at that point? And this is what it says: "Joint 'vojin.'"

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one before that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Do explain what this previous entry means. What is "BROM"? And what does this mean: "For operations ZZ."

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first entry -- well, I'm saying this not because it is written here. I'm saying it in that context because I remember this perfectly. The Army of Yugoslavia had quite a few batteries. "BROM" means "baterija raketa, obala, more," "battery of rockets, coast, sea." That's about 80 kilometres away. And they were taken out when the navy of the Yugoslav People's Army of the JNA was being withdrawn from its garrisons, from the military naval sector. That was the territory of the former Socialist Republic of Croatia. These rockets were not being used and were there, so we thought that we could perhaps use them, if necessary, as surface-to-surface rockets, they have the same kind of charge. And we were saying, If you don't have what we need, give us what you have. We will improvise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the last sentence of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that everything has been recorded, I think.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that everything --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- Just hold, ma'am, now that you have asked us to do something. Could all microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. You may proceed, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that if they did not have what it was that we were asking for, let them give us at least this and we will improvise on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you get anything as far as these rockets were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next entry says: "Joint 'vojin.'" General, do you remember, does that reflect some of your words at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This accurately reflects my words at that meeting and at other meetings as well. I repeated that very often. The actual entry here -- or, I mean, even if it hadn't been written up. "Vojin" means what I said. Its main characteristic is that as a system for securing the air-space, it can only be efficient if organised in a larger area. What have you -- what business do you have detecting aircraft that have already entered a very limited air-space? You should try to observe that as far away as possible so that your own units can be on the ready in a state of full combat-readiness to react. That is why I said to General Perisic and to all other participants that from the Adriatic to Romania a joint system should be set up. Technically that was feasible, and that could have been efficient, and it could have improved things. I was hoping that they would understand that, that that improved the capacity of fighting enemy targets in the air-space of the Army of Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And was a joint "vojin" system set up?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the next point in this list was: "Joint PED and EI ..." What were you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this very well because this is not the first time that I talked about this. I spoke about this at other meetings as well. My war-time experience confirmed exactly what I knew from theory, and that was that the use of electronic means and counter-electronic warfare against the enemy meant just as much as the use of what we could describe as hardware, meaning tanks, infantry, and other types of resources of that kind. And I have to say that it was strange to me and incomprehensible. And I had an objection about this in terms of General Perisic for as long as I was on duty and that was: Why didn't he make sure as a professional military man to have this system organised jointly and to have all joint systems that could be of interest either to the Army of Yugoslavia, the JNA [as interpreted], or to our army. I knew, for example, of cases when people in the electronic surveillance battalion in the area of Prokuplje were monitoring on a monthly basis one to two foreign communications in the area of neighbouring states. But when combat started in my area, suddenly 700 networks would be activated, 700 radio networks would be activated. And I kept telling General Perisic, If you don't want a joint system, at least send these people of yours so that they can see how things look as far as electronic surveillance is concerned in war time. You will increase the value of those units in that way, and you will be of help to us there. The same thing applied to this PED. These are counter-electronic activities, and that means defence measures against the enemy electronic warfare, meaning electronic surveillance. I don't need to go into details. Jamming, ruses, and all these other techniques that are used. And I can speak quite openly here and say that at the time I was trying to explain both to Mr. Perisic and to Mr. Milosevic that this would be useful for the Army of Yugoslavia also if they wanted to monitor what was happening around them. And for us it could help us without any kind of participation in the war outside of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that would be massive or of a compromising nature. And I have to say, today even, that it was unclear to me why this was never done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already answered my next question with this, so I'm just going to ask: Is it that this didn't happen for as long as you were the commander of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, or did this not happen all the way until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was the commander of the Serbian Army of the Krajina, this did not happen; and it did not happen, as far as I know and which I absolutely believed is accurate, it did not happen until the end of the existence of the Army of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the next entry is: "To send officers to K." Is this accurately reflecting what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Officers should be sent to the corps units, to the Serbian Army of the Krajina. I think that this text -- well, these are not minutes. When you translate it officially, you will see that these are notes made by one man. If I happened to have my notebook handy here, it would have been different. Evidently, if these are entries made by General Mladic, this is actually not everything that I said. I actually said, Send officers to corps units of the Serbian army of the Krajina. But we only have three dots here after that entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then after the text that follows, we have the name of President Milosevic. It's a longer section, but we can begin, at least, to go through it, even if we don't have too much time left for today. Well, I don't need to read the first three sentences, and there's nothing here to be disputed regarding the translation. I'm asking you: According to your recollection does this accurately reflect the words of President Milosevic? First answer that.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually remember exactly what this refers to because besides what is written here there was also a request made of me. Mr. Milosevic here is dealing with the internal political situation in Serbia, and as you can see there were internal enemies and 5th column elements in Serbia which were being programmed, as he put it, by the foreign factor, external factor. What is interesting is that in that period - and I know this perfectly well, and this is also something that can be seen in this entry here - the most dangerous opponent in the internal plan was viewed to be Mr. Seselj and the Serbian Radical Party because it was on the ascent and in that part of the political arena which Mr. Milosevic felt belonged to him. I remember that at one point in time I, as the commander of the Army of the Serbian Krajina and immediately after this, which affirms what I'm saying here and what is said here, was asked to blacken the reputation of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who were coming to fight in the area of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina in a public statement. So I read a public announcement at a session of the Assembly, which happened to be very tumultuous. I was asked to do that. Of course, I didn't do that because I felt and I said that the volunteers who were coming to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina to help in its defence we did not judge by their party affiliation; we saw them all as being equal, who were coming to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who asked you to read this public announcement?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I think it was the then-president of the Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to continue with this document, but I think it would be good to stop here, Your Honours, because we're about to change to another topic but remain on this document. Just one moment. Perhaps I have one intervention to the transcript. Just give me a minute, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't wish to interrupt the General, but Mr. Zorko is indicating to me now that on page 73, Your Honours -- page 73, line 8, when the witness was talking about the AE and the PED system, he said it was in the interest of the Army of Yugoslavia, the VRS, and my army, and what is said there is the JNA. So I just assume that it's a mistake in the transcript because the JNA was not actually mentioned in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see PED at line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's talking about that topic. You can see the question on line 20 in the previous page. He's talking about this system, EI and the PED; and then in his reply, page 73, line 8, what is written is the JNA, but he actually referred to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, absolutely. The JNA didn't exist at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the end for the day -- end of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I would like to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, unfortunately we are not going to be sitting tomorrow for logistical reasons within the Tribunal. We will sit on Monday in the afternoon at 2.00 in the same courtroom. Once again, I remind you that you may not discuss the case with anybody and in particular not with your Defence counsel. And if you do have anything outside the case that you would like to talk to him about, try to get in touch with one of the Court Officers and arrange that. Okay? And they will tell you whether you may or may not talk to him. The Court stands adjourned to Monday, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
